stories-18-92-98-iron-and-molten-brass-b.title: Dhu l-Qarnayn Building the Iron and Molten Brass Gate Against Gog and Magog
stories-18-92-98-iron-and-molten-brass-b.note: Surah 18:92–98 depicts Dhu l-Qarnayn erecting a rampart of iron blocks and molten brass between two mountain cliffs to seal in Gog and Magog until the apocalyptic promise of the Lord, matching the sixth-century Syriac Alexander Legend.

discussion.view: Classical commentators such as Ibn Ishaq, al-Tabari, and al-Qurtubi identify Dhu l-Qarnayn as Alexander the Great (`al-Iskandar`) or a righteous world-conqueror who built an iron-and-brass barrier in the north.
discussion.reply: Historical records of Alexander of Macedon (356–323 BC) show a polytheistic Greek king who built no apocalyptic wall against Gog and Magog. The plot of a two-horned monotheistic king traveling to the ends of the earth and casting an iron-and-brass gate between two mountains against Gog and Magog was composed in Syriac in northern Mesopotamia shortly before Islam.

stories-18-92-98-iron-and-molten-brass-b.quranEn: [92] Then he followed (another) way of access [93] until, when he arrived (at the place) between the two barriers, he found on this side of them a people hardly able to understand (his) speech. [94] They said, “Dhū-l-Qarnayn! Surely Yajūj and Majūj are fomenting corruption on the earth. Shall we pay tribute to you on (the condition) that you construct a barrier between us and them?” [95] He said, “What my Lord has established me with is better. Help me with a force, (and) I shall construct a rampart between you and them. [96] Bring me blocks of iron!” – Until, when he had made level (the gap) between the two cliffs, he said, “Blow!” – Until, when he had made it a fire, he said, “Bring me (blocks of brass)! I will pour molten brass over it.” [97] So they were not able to surmount it, nor were they able (to make) a hole in it. [98] He said, “This is a mercy from my Lord. But when the promise of my Lord comes, He will shatter it. The promise of my Lord is true.”’
quranHighlights: construct a rampart between you and them. [96] Bring me blocks of iron!”
when he had made level (the gap) between the two cliffs, he said, “Blow!”
“Bring me (blocks of brass)! I will pour molten brass over it.”

stories-18-19-20-silver-coins-sent-to-bu.title: Waking After Centuries and Sending an Ancient Silver Coin to Buy Bread
stories-18-19-20-silver-coins-sent-to-bu.note: Surah 18:19–20 recounts the youths waking in their cave, supposing they slept a day, and sending one companion with their silver coin (`wariqikum`) to the city to buy food discreetly, matching the Syriac and Latin Seven Sleepers of Ephesus homilies.

discussion.view: Classical commentators such as al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir recount that the Companions of the Cave fled an idolatrous Roman emperor and were miraculously preserved in sleep for over three centuries as a sign of bodily resurrection.
discussion.reply: The narrative of Christian youths hiding in a cave near Ephesus under Emperor Decius (AD 249–251), waking under the Christian emperor Theodosius II (AD 408–450), and sending a companion into town with obsolete silver coins was a famous fifth- and sixth-century Christian hagiography preserved in the Syriac homilies of Jacob of Serugh (d. 521) and Gregory of Tours.

stories-18-19-20-silver-coins-sent-to-bu.quranEn: [19] So We raised them up (again) that they might ask questions among themselves. A speaker among them said, ‘How long have you remained (here)?’ Some said, ‘We have (only) remained (here) a day, or part of a day.’ Others said, ‘Your Lord knows how long you have remained (here). So send one of you with this paper (money) of yours to the city, and let him see which (part) of it (has the) purest food, and let him bring you a supply of it. But let him be astute, and let no one realize (who) you (are). [20] Surely they – if they become aware of you – they will stone you, or make you return to their creed, and then you will never prosper.’
quranHighlights: send one of you with this paper (money) of yours to the city, and let him see which (part) of it (has the) purest food, and let him bring you a supply of it

sources.title: Jacob of Serugh, Homily (memra) on the Youths of Ephesus
sources.workSub: Jacob of Serugh, Homily (memra) on the Youths of Ephesus
sources.en: One of the youths, named Yamlikhā, goes down to the city to assess the situation and buy food. As the young man enters Ephesus, he is startled by the sign of the cross on the city's gates; when he tries to buy bread, the locals are astounded by the old-fashioned coins he is trying to use and think that has found a hoard. When the news reaches the city's bishop, he summons the young man and inquires about his identity; when the young man relates that he and his companions hid during the time of Decius, the whole city rushes to the cave, to see them.
highlights: One of the youths, named Yamlikhā, goes down to the city to assess the situation and buy food
when he tries to buy bread, the locals are astounded by the old-fashioned coins he is trying to use

sources.title: Gregory of Tours, Passio Septem Dormientium
sources.workSub: Gregory of Tours, Passio Septem Dormientium
sources.en: They gave Malchus some silver coins and asked him to go into town to buy them some food and to bring back news. When Malchus came to the town (Ephesus), he was amazed, because the city-gate had the sign of the cross on it. He went to the market and tried to pay with coins stamped with the name of Decius. (8) When the people saw the silver coins, they thought that Malchus had found an ancient treasure trove and some men grabbed him and led him to the bishop Marinus and to the prefect. Although he was asked about the coins, he did not understand the situation and asked through tears about the emperor Decius.

stories-18-60-65-moses-servant-and-reviv.title: Moses, His Young Servant, and the Salted Fish Reviving at the Spring
stories-18-60-65-moses-servant-and-reviv.note: Surah 18:60–65 narrates Moses and his young servant traveling to the junction of the two seas, where their dried fish revives and swims away into the water, matching the revived salted fish in Jacob of Serugh's Alexander discourse.

discussion.view: Muslim commentators and hadith (Sahih al-Bukhari 122) explain that Moses and his attendant Joshua set out with a salted fish in a basket as a divine sign to locate the sage al-Khidr at the meeting of the two seas.
discussion.reply: The Torah records the life of Moses and Joshua without any journey to the junction of two seas or a revived fish. In Late Antiquity, the episode in which a traveler's cook washes a dried salted fish at the Fountain of Life and watches it come to life and escape belongs to the Alexander Romance tradition, preserved in the Syriac discourse of Jacob of Serugh (d. AD 521; cf. the spring-washing variant in Talmud Tamid 32b).

stories-18-60-65-moses-servant-and-reviv.quranEn: [60] (Remember) when Moses said to his young man, ‘I shall not give up until I reach the junction of the two seas, or (else) I shall go on for a long time.’ [61] When they reached the junction of them, they forgot their fish, (for) it had taken its way into the sea, swimming off. [62] So when they had passed beyond (that place), he said to his young man, ‘Bring us our morning meal. We have indeed become weary from this journey of ours.’ [63] He said, ‘Did you see when we took refuge at the rock? Surely I forgot the fish – none other than Satan made me forget to remember it – and it took its way into the sea – an amazing thing!’ [64] He said, ‘That is what we were seeking!’ So they returned, retracing their footsteps. [65] And they found a servant, one of Our servants to whom We had given mercy from Us, and whom We had taught knowledge from Us.
quranHighlights: When they reached the junction of them, they forgot their fish, (for) it had taken its way into the sea, swimming off.
Surely I forgot the fish – none other than Satan made me forget to remember it – and it took its way into the sea

phrases-18-23-24-unless-god-wills-condit.title: 'Do Not Say of Anything: I Will Do That Tomorrow, Except: If God Pleases'
phrases-18-23-24-unless-god-wills-condit.note: Surah 18:23–24 commands 'Do not say of anything, Surely I am going to do that tomorrow, except: If God pleases,' matching James 4:13–15 ('Today or tomorrow we will go... Instead, you ought to say, If the Lord wills, we will live and also do this').

discussion.view: Commentators record that these verses admonished the Prophet after he promised to answer three questions from Meccan challengers 'tomorrow' without adding 'If God wills.'
discussion.reply: The two-part rhetorical structure—forbidding the statement 'I will do that tomorrow' and prescribing the exact conditional formula 'If the Lord wills, we will... do this or that'—matches the Greek New Testament Epistle of James (4:13–15), written in the first century AD.

phrases-18-23-24-unless-god-wills-condit.quranEn: [23] And do not say of anything, ‘Surely I am going to do that tomorrow,’ [24] except (with the proviso): ‘If God pleases.’ And remember your Lord, when you forget, and say, ‘It may be that my Lord will guide me to something nearer the right (way) than this.’
quranHighlights: And do not say of anything, ‘Surely I am going to do that tomorrow,’
except (with the proviso): ‘If God pleases.’

sources.title: Epistle of James (NASB)
sources.en: Come now, you who say, "Today or tomorrow we will go to such and such a city, and spend a year there and engage in business and make a profit." Yet you do not know what your life will be like tomorrow. You are [just] a vapor that appears for a little while and then vanishes away. Instead, [you ought] to say, "If the Lord wills, we will live and also do this or that."

stories-18-32-44-parable-arrogant-vineya.title: Parable of the Boastful Vineyard Owner Whose Lush Estate Is Ruined
stories-18-32-44-parable-arrogant-vineya.note: Surah 18:32–44 portrays a rich man boasting over two hedged grape gardens before his harvest is ruined overnight, combining Jesus' Parable of the Rich Fool in Luke 12:16–21 with the hedged vineyard laid waste in Isaiah 5:1–6.

discussion.view: Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report from early exegetes that the parable of the two garden owners in 18:32–44 illustrates a believer and a disbeliever among the ancients (often identified as two brothers among the Israelites) to warn Mecca's wealthy elite.
discussion.reply: The Quranic parable merges two canonical biblical passages: Isaiah 5:1–6, where a fertile vineyard hedged and planted with choice vines is laid waste when rain is withheld, and Luke 12:16–21, where a rich landowner boasts to his soul over his stored harvest on the very night his life and estate are stripped away.

stories-18-32-44-parable-arrogant-vineya.quranEn: [32] Strike for them a parable of two men: We made for one of them two gardens of grapes, and surrounded both with date palms, and placed between them (a field of) crops. [33] Each of the two gardens produced its fruit and did not fail in any way. And We caused a river to gush forth between them. [34] And he had fruit. So he said to his companion, while he was talking with him, ‘I am greater than you in wealth, and mightier in family.’ [35] And he entered his garden, doing himself evil, (for) he said, ‘I do not think that this will ever perish, [36] nor do I think the Hour is coming. If indeed I am returned to my Lord, I shall indeed find a better (place of) return than this.’ [37] His companion said to him, while he was talking with him, ‘Do you disbelieve in Him who created you from dust, then from a drop, (and) then fashioned you as a man? [38] But as for us, He is God, my Lord, and I do not associate anyone with my Lord. [39] Why did you not say, when you entered your garden, “What God pleases,” (for there is) no power except in God? If you see me as inferior to you in wealth and children, [40] it may be that my Lord will give me (something) better than your garden, and send on it a reckoning from the sky, so that it becomes slippery soil, [41] or its water sinks (into the earth), so that you will not be able to find it.’ [42] And (all) his fruit was overwhelmed, and in the morning he began wringing his hands over what he had spent on it, (for) it had collapsed on its trellises, and he said, ‘I wish I had not associated anyone with my Lord!’ [43] But there was no cohort to help him, other than God, and he was helpless. [44] In such a case protection (belongs only) to God, the True One. He is best in reward, and best in final outcome.
quranHighlights: We made for one of them two gardens of grapes, and surrounded both with date palms
And he entered his garden, doing himself evil, (for) he said, ‘I do not think that this will ever perish
And (all) his fruit was overwhelmed, and in the morning he began wringing his hands

sources.en: And He told them a parable, saying, "The land of a rich man was very productive. "And he began reasoning to himself, saying, 'What shall I do, since I have no place to store my crops?' "Then he said, 'This is what I will do: I will tear down my barns and build larger ones, and there I will store all my grain and my goods. 'And I will say to my soul, "Soul, you have many goods laid up for many years [to come]; take your ease, eat, drink [and] be merry."' "But God said to him, 'You fool! stories-18-83-91-dhu-l-qarnayn-setting-a.title: Dhu l-Qarnayn Reaching the Muddy Spring of the Setting Sun and the East
stories-18-83-91-dhu-l-qarnayn-setting-a.note: Surah 18:83–91 narrates Dhu l-Qarnayn ('The Two-Horned One') traveling to the sun's setting place in a muddy spring and to its rising place over a shelterless people, matching the journeys of Alexander the Great in the Syriac Christian Legend.

discussion.view: Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir record early reports identifying Dhu l-Qarnayn as a righteous world-conqueror granted divine pathways across the earth, explaining 'setting in a muddy spring' as either how the western ocean appeared to his eye or the sun's literal western station.
discussion.reply: In the early seventh-century Syriac Christian Legend Concerning Alexander, Alexander prays to God as the king upon whose head God placed two horns to thrust down the kingdoms of the world, marches to the fetid western sea where the sun enters the window of heaven, and travels east to the people who have no shelter from the rising sun's heat.

stories-18-83-91-dhu-l-qarnayn-setting-a.quranEn: [83] They ask you about Dhū-l-Qarnayn. Say: ‘I shall recite to you a remembrance of him. [84] Surely We established him on the earth and gave him a way of access to everything. [85] He followed (one such) way of access [86] until, when he reached the setting of the sun, he found it setting in a muddy spring, and he found next to it a people. We said, “Dhū-l-Qarnayn! Either punish (them) or do them (some) good.” [87] He said, “As for the one who does evil, we shall punish him. Then he will be returned to his Lord, and He will punish him (with) a terrible punishment. [88] But as for the one who believes, and does righteousness, for him (there is) the good payment, and we shall speak to him something easy from our command.” [89] Then he followed (another) way of access [90] until, when he reached the rising (place) of the sun, he found it rising on a people for whom We had not provided any shelter from it. [91] So (it was), but We had already encompassed what his situation was in (our) awareness.
quranHighlights: They ask you about Dhū-l-Qarnayn.
when he reached the setting of the sun, he found it setting in a muddy spring
when he reached the rising (place) of the sun, he found it rising on a people for whom We had not provided any shelter from it.

phrases-18-109-if-the-sea-were-ink.title: 'If the Sea Were Ink for the Words of My Lord, the Sea Would Give Out'
phrases-18-109-if-the-sea-were-ink.note: Surah 18:109 states 'If the sea were ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would indeed give out before the words of my Lord would give out,' matching Rabbi Eliezer's formula in Midrash Shir HaShirim Rabbah 1:3.

discussion.view: Muslim exegetes view this verse as a divine command instructing the Prophet to illustrate the infinite scope of God's knowledge to his questioners.
discussion.reply: As in Surah 31:27, this verse adapts the rabbinic hyperbole preserved in Shir HaShirim Rabbah 1:3 and Talmud Bavli Shabbat 11a ('If all the seas were ink... they would not suffice to write the matters of Torah that I have learned'), elevating a rabbinic tribute to Torah scholarship into direct divine speech.

phrases-18-109-if-the-sea-were-ink.quranEn: Say: ‘If the sea were ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would indeed give out before the words of my Lord would give out, even if We brought (another sea) like it as an extension.’
quranHighlights: ‘If the sea were ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would indeed give out before the words of my Lord would give out, even if We brought (another sea) like it as an extension.’

sources.title: Midrash Shir HaShirim Rabbah
sources.en: Rabbi Eliezer says: If all the seas were ink, [all the reeds that grow in] the swamps were quills, the heavens and the earth were scrolls, and all people were scribes, they would not suffice to write the matters of Torah that I have learned [from my teachers], and I culled only the equivalent of one who dips the tip of his quill, like a brush, in the sea.
highlights: If all the seas were ink, [all the reeds that grow in] the swamps were quills, the heavens and the earth were scrolls, and all people were scribes, they would not suffice to write the matters of Torah
sources.orig: רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר אוֹמֵר, אִם יִהְיוּ כָּל הַיַּמִּים דְּיוֹ, וַאֲגַמִּים קוּלְמוֹסִין, וְשָׁמַיִם וְאֶרֶץ מְגִלּוֹת, וְכָל בְּנֵי הָאָדָם לַבְלָרִים, אֵין מַסְפִּיקִין לִכְתּוֹב [דברי תורה שלמדתי], וַאֲנִי לֹא חִסַּרְתִּיהָ אֶלָּא כְּאָדָם שֶׁמַּטְבִּיל זַכְרוּתוֹ כְּמִכְּחוֹל בַּיָּם.

stories-18-22-disputing-sleepers-number-.title: Rival Claims Over Whether the Sleepers of the Cave Were Seven or Eight
stories-18-22-disputing-sleepers-number-.note: Surah 18:22 catalogues rival claims over the headcount of the youths in the cave (three, five, or seven with their dog as the eighth), mirroring the split between eight youths in Jacob of Serugh's Syriac homily and seven youths with a dog in Theodosius.

discussion.view: Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report from Ibn 'Abbas that Christian denominations of Najran and Syria disputed whether the sleepers numbered three, five, or seven alongside their dog Qitmir, and that 18:22 endorses the count of seven youths plus their dog.
discussion.reply: Late antique Christian sources preserve the exact numerical divergence cited in 18:22: West-Syrian bishop Jacob of Serugh (d. 521) consistently numbers the youths of Ephesus as eight companions in his Syriac memra, whereas the Greek and Latin tradition represents them as seven brothers, to whom the sixth-century pilgrim Theodosius (De situ terrae sanctae 26) adds the dog Viricanus at their feet.

stories-18-22-disputing-sleepers-number-.quranEn: Some say, ‘(There were) three, the fourth of them was their dog.’ But others say, ‘(There were) five, the sixth of them was their dog’ – guessing about what is unknown. Still others say, ‘(There were) seven, the eighth of them was their dog.’ Say: ‘My Lord knows about their number. No one knows (about) them except a few.’ So do not dispute about them, except (on) an obvious point, and do not ask for a pronouncement about them from any of them.
quranHighlights: Some say, ‘(There were) three, the fourth of them was their dog.’
‘(There were) five, the sixth of them was their dog’
‘(There were) seven, the eighth of them was their dog.’

sources.title: Jacob of Serugh, Homily (memra) on the Youths of Ephesus
sources.workSub: Jacob of Serugh, Homily (memra) on the Youths of Ephesus
sources.en: When the emperor Decius visits the city of Ephesus, he builds temples to several pagan deities and demands that the citizens offer sacrifices there; a group of eight Christian young men refuse to comply and are threatened with court action. When Decius leaves Ephesus for a while, the youths hide in a cave on the mountain in the city's vicinity, where God 'took their spirits and raised them up above, to heaven, and left a watcher to be guarding their limbs.' When Decius returns to the city, he orders the youths to be immured in the cave.
highlights: a group of eight Christian young men refuse to comply
the youths hide in a cave on the mountain in the city's vicinity

stories-18-9-12-sleepers-sealed-in-cave.title: The Companions of the Cave and al-Raqim Sealed in Sleep for Years
stories-18-9-12-sleepers-sealed-in-cave.note: Surah 18:9–12 introduces the youths of the Cave and al-Raqim (the inscription) whose ears are sealed in sleep for generations before awakening, matching Gregory of Tours' account of the lead tablets placed at the sealed entrance of the Ephesian cave.

discussion.view: Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir record multiple early explanations of al-Raqim in 18:9, with Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and Wahb ibn Munabbih identifying it as an inscribed tablet of stone or lead recording the names and story of the youths at the cave entrance.
discussion.reply: Distinctive to 18:9–12 is the pairing of 'the Companions of the Cave and al-Raqim' (ashaba l-kahfi wa-l-raqim) with the sealing of their ears in sleep. In the sixth-century Passio Septem Dormientium of Gregory of Tours (translated from Syriac), two Christians named Theodore and Ruben write the history of the youths on lead tablets and place them inside the blocked mouth of the cave.

stories-18-9-12-sleepers-sealed-in-cave.quranEn: [9] Or did you think that the companions of the cave and al-Raqīm were an amazing thing among Our signs? [10] (Remember) when the young men took refuge in the cave, and said, ‘Our Lord, grant us mercy from Yourself, and furnish the right (course) for us in our situation.’ [11] So We sealed up their ears in the cave for a number of years, [12] and then We raised them up (again), so that We might know which of the two factions would better count (the length of) time (they had) remained (there).
quranHighlights: the companions of the cave and al-Raqīm
when the young men took refuge in the cave
So We sealed up their ears in the cave for a number of years

sources.title: Gregory of Tours, Passio Septem Dormientium
sources.ref: Sections 5-6 (trans. with John the Syrian; Oxford CSLA E05364)
sources.workSub: Gregory of Tours, Passio Septem Dormientium
sources.en: When the emperor was informed that they were staying in this cave, he ordered that the mouth of the cave be blocked off. Two Christians, Theodore and Ruben went ahead of the men who were supposed to block up the cave’s opening, and wrote on some lead tablets the whole history of the men and placed these inside the entrance to the cave. After many years, Theodosius became the emperor. In his times the sect of the Sadduccees arose and sought to persuade the emperor of the falsehood of the resurrection.

stories-18-13-16-youths-defying-idolatro.title: Believing Youths Standing Before the Pagan Ruler and Fleeing to the Cave
stories-18-13-16-youths-defying-idolatro.note: Surah 18:13–16 narrates how the believing youths stood up to proclaim that their Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth, rejected their people's idols, and withdrew into the cave, matching Gregory of Tours' account of the youths defying Decius.

discussion.view: Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir recount that the youths were noble sons of Ephesus who stood before the idolatrous king Daqyanus (Decius), refused to offer pagan sacrifices, and fled to a mountain cave outside the city to preserve their faith.
discussion.reply: Whereas 18:9–12 summarizes the sleep in the cave and 18:17–20 describes their awakening and silver coin, 18:13–16 focuses on their public confession before the pagan court (idh qamu fa-qalu Rabbuna Rabbu l-samawati wa-l-ard). Gregory of Tours' sixth-century Latin Passio (translated from a fifth-century Syriac original) opens with the noble youths arrested before Emperor Decius, refusing pagan sacrifice, and retreating to the cave.

stories-18-13-16-youths-defying-idolatro.quranEn: [13] We shall recount to you their story in truth: Surely they were young men who believed in their Lord, and We increased them in guidance. [14] We strengthened their hearts, when they stood up and said, ‘Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth. We do not call on any god other than Him. Certainly we would then have spoken an outrageous thing. [15] These people of ours have taken gods other than Him. If only they would bring some clear authority concerning them! Who is more evil than the one who forges a lie against God? [16] When you have withdrawn from them and what they serve instead of God, take refuge in the cave. Your Lord will display some of His mercy to you, and will furnish some relief for you in your situation.’
quranHighlights: when they stood up and said, ‘Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth. We do not call on any god other than Him.
When you have withdrawn from them and what they serve instead of God, take refuge in the cave.

sources.title: Gregory of Tours, Passio Septem Dormientium
sources.ref: Sections 1-4 (trans. with John the Syrian; Oxford CSLA E05364)
sources.workSub: Gregory of Tours, Passio Septem Dormientium
sources.en: During the reign of the emperor Decius there was a persecution against the Christians. At that time seven men from prominent families, named Maximianus, Malchus, Martinianus, Constantinus, Dionysius, Johannes, and Serapion were arrested and investigated before the emperor. Although threatened and ordered to sacrifice to the pagan gods, they refused. (3) They were granted some time to think and change their minds, while the emperor visited another city; they sold their possessions and gave the proceeds to the poor, and withdrew to a cave on Mount Celion, selecting Malchus to go in secret to the city to purchase supplies. (4) When they learned that the emperor, on his return, had asked about them, they became scared and prayed, and God set them in a deep slumber.

withdrew to a cave on Mount Celion

stories-18-21-sanctuary-built-over-sleep.title: The Resurrection Proof and Building a Sanctuary Over the Sleepers' Cave
stories-18-21-sanctuary-built-over-sleep.note: Surah 18:21 states that the sleepers were discovered to confirm the resurrection of the dead, after which the authorities resolved to build a sanctuary (masjidan) over their cave, matching Gregory of Tours' Passio on Emperor Theodosius II.

discussion.view: Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that God caused the citizens to discover the youths so the king and his divided subjects would know that bodily resurrection is true, after which the prevailing party built a sanctuary over the cave entrance.
discussion.reply: Surah 18:21 preserves two specific narrative elements from the Christian legend of Ephesus: first, that the awakening took place specifically to settle a theological controversy over the bodily resurrection under Emperor Theodosius II; and second, that after the youths fell asleep again, the authorities proposed building a shrine or basilica (basilica magna) directly over their bodies at the cave.

stories-18-21-sanctuary-built-over-sleep.quranEn: So We caused (the people of the city) to stumble upon them, in order that they might know that the promise of God is true, and that the Hour – (there is) no doubt about it. When they argued among themselves about their situation, they said, ‘Build over them a building. Their Lord knows about them.’ Those who prevailed over their situation said, ‘We shall indeed take (to building) a place of worship over them.’

sources.title: Gregory of Tours, Passio Septem Dormientium
sources.workSub: Gregory of Tours, Passio Septem Dormientium
sources.en: Then Maximianus said that therefore all should believe in the resurrection of the dead, after which the saints lay down again and slept upon the earth. The Emperor saw these things and crying placed his own clothes over the martyrs and ordered golden coffins to be made for them. But that night the saints appeared to him and told him to leave them above the ground. Then Theodosius constructed a great church (basilica magna) above them, and there made a hospice (receptaculum) for the poor. And, when the bishops had assembled, he celebrated their feast.
